abstract: This lecture covers common genital infections in both males and females, including bacterial vaginosis, herpes simplex virus, gonorrhea, chlamydia, trichomoniasis, and syphilis. The speaker emphasizes diagnostic criteria such as the Amsel criteria for bacterial vaginosis, the importance of distinguishing primary from recurrent HSV for treatment decisions, and the clinical presentation of gonorrhea/chlamydia with endocervical discharge. Key teaching points include the role of pH in vaginal infections, the necessity of physical exam for herpes lesions in pregnancy, and the high prevalence of syphilis in Oklahoma.
key_points: Bacterial vaginosis diagnosis requires three of four Amsel criteria: thin milky discharge, pH >4.5, positive whiff test, and clue cells on wet prep.
Normal vaginal pH is ≤4.5, maintained by lactobacillus; elevated pH from semen, menses, or trichomonas predisposes to bacterial vaginosis.
Primary HSV infection is treated more aggressively than recurrent episodes and can cause systemic symptoms requiring hospitalization.
In pregnancy with active herpetic lesions near delivery, cesarean section is indicated to prevent neonatal transmission.
Gonorrhea and chlamydia are intracellular organisms in columnar cells of the endocervix, producing purulent discharge from the cervical os.
When the specific organism is unknown, presumptive treatment for both gonorrhea and chlamydia is recommended.
Trichomoniasis presents with frothy yellow-green discharge, vaginal irritation, postcoital spotting, and strawberry cervix on exam.
Syphilis rash can be subtle, variable in appearance, and may be transient; testing is essential if syphilis is suspected.
Pearly penile papules and Fordyce spots are benign and distinguished from genital warts by their soft texture and lack of hardness.
Asymptomatic HSV transmission can occur when lesions are present but painless; daily suppressive therapy reduces recurrence and transmission risk.
